name: Cherry Picking
shortDef: Citing only the evidence that supports you and ignoring the rest.
definition: Presenting the data points, studies, quotes or time periods that favor a conclusion while leaving out or waving away the available evidence that cuts against it, so the case looks stronger than it is.
howToSpot: Is this all the evidence, or just the best-looking slice of it?
Why does the time period, group or sample start and stop where it does?
What would the full dataset, average or overall rating show?
classicExample: Our fund returned 31% last year! (The small print: losses in two of the four years before that.)
legitimateVersion: Focusing on a subset is fair when the rule for choosing it is set in advance and applied evenly, such as excluding low-quality studies, and when including everything wouldn't change the conclusion.

contrast.fal_texas_sharpshooter: Cherry picking hides or ignores unfavorable evidence; the sharpshooter finds a cluster after the fact and treats it as the target all along.
contrast.fal_hasty_generalization: Cherry picking chooses the favorable cases from many available; hasty generalization leans on too few cases to begin with.
